Makkan, and its verses number 26 [revealed after Surah al-Dhariyat].

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Al-Ghashiyah﴾: the calamity that overwhelms people with its hardships and clothes them in its terrors. It means the Resurrection, from His saying ﴿The Day the punishment will overwhelm them﴾. It was also said that it means the Fire, from His saying ﴿and the Fire will cover their faces﴾, and ﴿above them will be coverings of fire﴾.

﴿On that Day﴾: the day when it overwhelms.

﴿Downcast﴾: humbled.

﴿Labouring, weary﴾: laboring in the Fire at a task that wearies them. This is their dragging of chains and shackles. [Mahmud said: "Humbled, laboring in the Fire at a task that exhausts them, which is their dragging of chains..." etc. Ahmad said: The first interpretation is the necessary one, because the adverbial phrase mentioned, which is His saying ﴿on that Day﴾, is cut off from the clause to which it is attached. Its implied form is: "the day when it overwhelms." That refers to the Hereafter without any difficulty, and it is an adverb governing all the attributes predicated, namely: downcast, laboring, weary. So how could it encompass the deeds of this world?]

Their wading in the Fire as camels wade through mud, their hurried ascent in a climb of fire, and their descent down a slope of it. It was also said: they labored and toiled in evil deeds in this world and took pleasure and delight in them, so in the Hereafter they are in weariness because of them. It was also said: they labored and toiled at deeds that will profit them nothing in the Hereafter, from His saying ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust. Those who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, their deeds are worthless﴾. It was also said: they are the people of the monasteries. The meaning is that they were humbled before God, and labored and toiled in their practices, such as continual fasting [al-sawm al-da'ib] and wearisome night prayer [al-tahajjud al-wasib]. [Note: "al-da'ib" and "al-wasib" both mean "constant."(ʿ)]

It has been read as ﴿laboring, weary﴾ in the accusative of reproach [al-shatm].

It has been read as ﴿they will burn [tuslā]﴾ with an open tā', with a damma on the tā', and with a shadda on the ṣād.

According to the Arabs, al-muṣallā [the one burned] is that they dig a pit, gather a great deal of embers into it, then deliberately put a sheep in the middle. As for what is roasted over embers, on a griddle, or in an oven, it is not called muṣallā.

﴿Boiling hot﴾: intensely hot, as in His saying ﴿between it and burning hot water﴾ [ḥamīm ānin].

﴿Dhari': thorny plant.

Dhari' is the dried-up shibriq, a kind of thorn that camels graze on while it is still moist. When it dries out, camels avoid it, and it is a deadly poison. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

It grazed on the lush shibriq until it withered, and became dhari', and the barren she-camels left it.

[Meaning: the camel grazed on lush shibriq, that is moist thorn. Dhawā (withered) means it dried up. Dhawā like riḍā: al-Jawhari rejected this, but Abu 'Ubayda affirmed it. That is, when it dried and became dry, crumbling dhari', the barren she-camels left it, meaning it does not fatten them and does not satisfy hunger.]

And he said:

They were confined amid the dry dhari', so all of them were humped, bleeding-handed from thorns, emaciated.

[This is by Qays ibn 'Ayzara. Hazmuhu (with a zayn) means broken. A hazmā' she-camel is one whose hip bones show from emaciation. Al-harm (with a rā') is the ḥamḍ plant, and a 'ārim camel grazes on ḥamḍ. Dhari' is an ugly thorny plant. Ḥadab is bending, and ḥadbā' is bent over. Ḥarada means dried up and parched. He says: the she-camels were confined in pasture that is poor and crumbling, so all of them were humped in the back or legs from emaciation, bleeding-handed from thorns, and giving little milk.]

If you ask: why is it said ﴿They will have no food but dhari'﴾, while in al-Haqqah it is said ﴿nor any food except from ghislin﴾?

I say: punishment has many kinds, and the tormented are of different classes. Among them are those who eat the zaqqum, among them those who eat ghislin, and among them those who eat dhari': ﴿For every gate of them is an allotted portion﴾. [It does not fatten nor satisfy hunger.] Its place in the grammar is either raised or in the genitive, as a description of food, or dhari', meaning: their food is from a thing that is not among human foods. It is only thorn, and thorn is among what camels graze on and are fond of. This is a kind of it from which they recoil and do not approach. The two benefits of food are absent from it: removing hunger and providing strength and fattening the body. Or it is meant that they have no food at all, because dhari' is not food even for beasts, let alone humans, since food is what satisfies or fattens, and it is far from both. Just as you say, "So-and-so has no shade except the sun," meaning: the negation of shade is emphatic.

It was also said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "Indeed, our camels grow fat on dhari'," so this was revealed: ﴿does not fatten﴾. Then it is either that they lied and sought to provoke with that, which is the apparent reading, so their claim is refuted by denying fattening and satisfaction, or that they are truthful, in which case the meaning is: their food is from a dhari' that is not of the kind of your dhari', but from a dhari' that neither fattens nor satisfies hunger.

**﴿Joyful﴾**, possessing radiance and beauty, like His saying: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾. Or, **﴿enjoying comfort﴾**. ﴿Content with their striving﴾: pleased with their deeds when they saw what they had been brought to of honor and reward. ﴿In a lofty garden﴾, lofty in place or in rank. ﴿Where they will hear no idle talk﴾, O addressee. Or, the faces are ﴿idle﴾, meaning frivolous. Or, a soul that engages in idle talk. The people of Paradise speak only with wisdom and praise God for the everlasting bliss He has bestowed upon them. It is also read:

**﴿Not heard﴾**, in the passive voice, with both the ta and the ya. [[His saying "in the passive voice with the ta and the ya": i.e., "lāghiyatun" with raf' in both.  (ʿ)]] ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾, meaning springs in the greatest abundance, like His saying: ﴿Every soul will know﴾. ﴿Raised high﴾, in elevation of rank or height, so that the believer, by sitting upon it, sees all that his Lord has granted him of dominion and bliss. It is said: ﴿Placed﴾, hidden for them, from *rafaʿa* (to lift) meaning *khabaʾa* (to conceal). ﴿And cups set out﴾, whenever they wish for them they find them placed before them, ready and present, so they need not ask for them. Or, placed on the edges of the springs, prepared for drinking. It is also permissible to mean: placed beyond the measure of large sizes, medium between small and large, like His saying: ﴿They measured it with measure﴾. ﴿And cushions arranged﴾, some beside others. ﴿Cushions and ...﴾ [[His phrase "cushions and ...": this is the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]], wherever he wishes to sit, on a cushion, and lean upon another. ﴿And carpets﴾, broad and luxurious spreads. It is said: they are the rugs that have a fine nap, plural of *zarabiyyah*. ﴿Spread out﴾, laid out.

Will they not look at the camels, how they were created—a wondrous creation, pointing to a determining Decreer, a witness to the arrangement of an Arranger—since He created them for rising up under burdens and for dragging them to far-off lands? [[Commentary: "to far-off lands" means distant ones. Stated in al-Sihah. (Editor's note: ʿ)]] So He made them kneel until they bear loads with ease and nearness, then they rise with what they have carried. He made them subservient, submitting to whoever leads them by their reins: they do not overpower the weak nor resist the young. He formed them with long necks so that they may bear heavy loads. It is related from some of the wise that he spoke about the camel and its wondrous creation, though he had grown up in lands with no camels. He reflected and then said: "It is likely that they have long necks." And when He willed that they be ships of the desert, He made them patient in enduring thirst, so that their intervals between watering [[Commentary: "their intervals" — in al-Sihah, "al-zamaʾ" is the span between two waterings, namely the keeping of camels away from water until the time of watering; the plural is "al-azmaʾ." (Editor's note: ʿ)]] extend to ten days or more, and He made them graze on everything that grows in the wilderness and the deserts, things that other beasts do not graze on. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: "I met the judge Shurayh and I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'I am going to al-Kunasah.' I said: 'What will you do there?' He said: 'I will look at the camels, how they were created.'"

If you ask: how is the mention of camels appropriate alongside the sky, the mountains and the earth, with no connection? I say: the Arabs' gaze in their valleys and deserts has linked these things together, so the mention links them according to the way their gaze links them. Whoever claimed that "the camels" means the clouds, [...] did so only out of seeking a connection. Perhaps he did not mean that "camels" is one of the names of clouds, like "ghamam," "muzn," "rabab," "ghaym," "ghayn," and others; rather, he saw the cloud often likened to camels in their poetry, so he allowed that it be meant by them in the manner of simile and metaphor.

"How it was raised high, raised to a far extent, by holding it up without pillars." "How it was set up, set firmly, so it stands and does not incline or move." "How it was spread out, smoothed and prepared, so it is a resting-place for one who lies upon it."

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "khuliqat, rufiʿat, nusibat, and suthihat" with the active verb and the ta' of the subject, the implied sense being: "You (God) did (them)," so the object was omitted. It is related from Harun al-Rashid that he read "suthihat" with the doubled sע (tashdid).

The meaning: Will they not look at these created things that bear witness to the power of the Creator, so that they do not deny His capacity to resurrect, and so that they hear the warning of the Messenger ﷺ, believe in him, and prepare for meeting Him? "You are not over them a controller" (88:22)—not one who dominates them—like His saying: "You are not over them a tyrant" (50:45). It was said: in the dialect of Tamim the vowel of the ta' is fatha, so that "sayṭara" is transitive for them; and their saying "tusayṭir" supports this. "Except one who turns away and disbelieves" (88:23): an exceptive clause of disconnection, meaning: you are not one who has control over them, but whoever turns away and disbelieves among them—for God holds the authority and power. "So God will punish him with the greatest punishment" (88:24), which is the punishment of hell. It was said: it is an exception from His saying "so remind" (88:21), meaning: remind, except whoever your hope of his faith has been cut off from, and who turns away, so he deserves the greatest punishment; and what lies between is a parenthetical clause. It is read "illa man tawalla" with the particle of alerting. In Ibn Masʿud's reading: "fa-innahu yuʿadhdhibuhu."

"Except one who turns away and disbelieves" (88:23): an exceptive clause of disconnection, meaning: you are not one who has control over them, but whoever turns away and disbelieves among them—for God holds the authority and power. It is read "illa man tawalla" with the particle of alerting. In Ibn Masʿud's reading: "fa-innahu yuʿadhdhibuhu."

I say: its meaning is emphasis in the threat, and that their return is only to the Almighty, capable of retribution, and that their reckoning is obligatory only upon Him, who reckons even the smallest speck. The meaning of "obligation" is obligation in wisdom. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Ghashiyah, Allah will reckon with him an easy reckoning." [[Reported by al-Wahidi, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]

Will they not look at the camels, how they were created—a wondrous creation, pointing to a determining Decreer, a witness to the arrangement of an Arranger—since He created them for rising up under burdens and for dragging them to far-off lands? [[Commentary: "to far-off lands" means distant ones. Stated in al-Sihah. (Editor's note: ʿ)]] So He made them kneel until they bear loads with ease and nearness, then they rise with what they have carried. He made them subservient, submitting to whoever leads them by their reins: they do not overpower the weak nor resist the young. He formed them with long necks so that they may bear heavy loads. It is related from some of the wise that he spoke about the camel and its wondrous creation, though he had grown up in lands with no camels. He reflected and then said: "It is likely that they have long necks." And when He willed that they be ships of the desert, He made them patient in enduring thirst, so that their intervals between watering [[Commentary: "their intervals" — in al-Sihah, "al-zamaʾ" is the span between two waterings, namely the keeping of camels away from water until the time of watering; the plural is "al-azmaʾ." (Editor's note: ʿ)]] extend to ten days or more, and He made them graze on everything that grows in the wilderness and the deserts, things that other beasts do not graze on. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: "I met the judge Shurayh and I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'I am going to al-Kunasah.' I said: 'What will you do there?' He said: 'I will look at the camels, how they were created.'"

If you ask: how is the mention of camels appropriate alongside the sky, the mountains and the earth, with no connection? I say: the Arabs' gaze in their valleys and deserts has linked these things together, so the mention links them according to the way their gaze links them. Whoever claimed that "the camels" means the clouds, [...] did so only out of seeking a connection. Perhaps he did not mean that "camels" is one of the names of clouds, like "ghamam," "muzn," "rabab," "ghaym," "ghayn," and others; rather, he saw the cloud often likened to camels in their poetry, so he allowed that it be meant by them in the manner of simile and metaphor.

"How it was raised high, raised to a far extent, by holding it up without pillars." "How it was set up, set firmly, so it stands and does not incline or move." "How it was spread out, smoothed and prepared, so it is a resting-place for one who lies upon it."

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "khuliqat, rufiʿat, nusibat, and suthihat" with the active verb and the ta' of the subject, the implied sense being: "You (God) did (them)," so the object was omitted. It is related from Harun al-Rashid that he read "suthihat" with the doubled sע (tashdid).
